texto:
YouTube on November 13, 2026 made Insights, a plain-language layer that now fronts the Analytics section of YouTube Studio, available to creators on desktop, together with a Research tab that takes the place of the old Trends tab. The same day, Ask Studio, the conversational assistant built into YouTube Studio, arrived in the Studio mobile app on Android and iPhone, and gained the ability to read up to 10 uploaded images at once. The changes were set out in a video on Creator Insider, the YouTube-run channel for creator product news, titled "New! Ask Studio on Mobile, Image Uploads, Research Tab, Insights are the new Analytics" and in a YouTube Help Community post by Dave of TeamYouTube, a Google employee, both published on November 13.
In Short
YouTube has redesigned the stats section of its creator dashboard so that it explains, in sentences, why a channel's numbers moved, and it has swapped the old Trends tool for a Research tab that ranks other channels' unusually successful videos. Brands, agencies and creators who rely on those dashboards will see different screens, although YouTube says the detailed reports, advanced analytics and real-time data are all still there. The company's AI assistant for creators also works on phones now and can look at pictures, but YouTube has not said in detail which creators count as eligible.
Analytics becomes Insights
The biggest change is the one with the plainest name. "YouTube analytics is becoming insights shifting from dense raw data to clear plain language takeaways that explain the why behind the metrics accessible directly from the left navigation menu in Studio on desktop," the presenter says in the video, at 1:56.
The written announcement frames the change more cautiously. "We know that sometimes raw numbers and charts can be overwhelming. That's why we're updating the Analytics experience to include Insights, a new way to understand your channel's performance," according to the Community post. It then describes what the new layer surfaces: "Insights highlights the story behind your data in plain, natural language, showing you which videos brought in new viewers, where watch time peaked, and how your latest uploads are performing compared to your typical content."
Is this a replacement or an addition? The two sources lean in different directions. The video says Analytics "is becoming" Insights. The post says Insights is being included in the Analytics experience and adds: "Insights are designed to complement your existing data and Analytics tools, which are still fully available in Studio whenever you need them." YouTube's Help Center page "Get started with YouTube Insights" settles the naming question at least: it states that the Analytics page has been updated to the Insights page on desktop, reached from the left menu of Studio, or at video level through Content and then Insights.
Shelves, cards and a click to the tables
According to the video, Insights brings "streamlined layouts with metrics grouped into scannable shelves on your overview page," with the aim of "cutting visual clutter while keeping key numbers front and center." Creators who qualify for Ask Studio get an extra card on that page, described as "breaking down key channel trends, top video drivers, and audience behavior." The detail sits one layer down. "And for us analytics nerds, detailed tables and custom date ranges just a click away by selecting any card," the presenter says.
The image attached to the Community post shows how that looks in practice. An Insights heading sits above four buttons labelled Content, Audience, Revenue and Research, with an "Advanced mode" button in the top right corner. Key metrics can be switched between 7 days, 28 days and 90 days. Below the charts for views, watch time, subscribers and estimated revenue, a card written in plain English reads "Views are up thanks to loyal viewers watching your event recaps," with a link to view the report. The figures in the image belong to a demonstration channel.
What YouTube says is not changing
The presenter anticipates the objection before the comments arrive. "And yes, YouTube totally gets that this is a really big change. It's why advanced analytics and real time aren't changing." The reason for the rebuild is given in one sentence: "But the old system just wasn't flexible enough to keep evolving and to focus on important metrics like audience segments." The video closes with an invitation: "And if there's anything you're still really missing, please drop it in the comments."
That matters for anyone who uses Studio's deeper metrics. Several of the measures YouTube has added in the past year live in advanced mode. Unique Reach, an estimate of the individual people who saw a video, was announced on May 22, 2026. A views co-viewed metric, which estimates how many people watch together on a TV, was placed beside it in September. Both should stay where they were, if the video's assurance holds.
First reactions
By November 14, the video had drawn 4,431 views, 340 likes and 123 comments. Most of the visible comments thanked the team. The most-liked one, with 27 likes, came from a channel called CosplayCinematics and was a complaint: "Yesterday I found out my video analytics tabs are all gone." The commenter described having to click "Reach -> back -> Engagement -> back -> Audience -> back -> Revenue" to move between reports that used to sit side by side as tabs. The Community post had 26 replies, nearly all of them brief thanks.
A change four months in the making
Insights did not arrive unannounced. On July 17, 2026, Net Influencer reported on a July 16 post by YouTube staff on the YouTube Community forum describing a test for a limited group of creators. In that test, according to Net Influencer, the Analytics tab was renamed Insights, four AI cards named Channel Summary, Content Patterns, Audience Loyalty and Video Summary appeared for creators eligible for Ask Studio, the overview page got a simpler date selector while custom date ranges stayed available through Advanced Mode, and the Trends tab became Research. The same report said saved keywords on desktop were being retired, with three months for creators to download them as a CSV file or keep using them in the mobile app.
YouTube's Help Center page on the Trends tab still carries a banner saying that, starting in July 2026, YouTube is gradually rolling out an updated YouTube Studio experience, so the tab may look different. At Made on YouTube on September 23, 2026, the company presented the upgrade on stage. A Creator Insider video from that event, covered by PPC Land on September 27, described Analytics in YouTube Studio as getting an upgrade to Insights and demonstrated Research as a tab inside Insights, without dates or markets.
The Community post published on November 13 refers back to that event: "At Made on YouTube in September, we highlighted the upcoming launch of new tools built to help you brainstorm ideas, plan content, and understand your audience." The rollout status is stated at the end of the post: "Ask Studio and Image Uploads are now available to eligible creators globally across desktop and the Studio mobile app, and Research and Insights are available on desktop devices."
The documentation has not fully caught up. The Insights help page still lists a Trends tab among the reports available from Insights, and links it to the help article that now describes Research. The Trends help page itself still tells creators to select Analytics in the left menu.
Research replaces Trends
"We are updating the Trends tab to a personalized, content-first destination called Research!" the Community post announces. It describes the tool as "powered by viewer data from your niche to help you turn what's working across YouTube into fresh concepts, titles, and thumbnails."
The video presents the same tool in the conditional, opening the segment with a question: "What if the old trends tab turned into a brand new research tab on desktop?" It goes on to describe "a personalized content first feed built to help you explore and validate ideas before you start creating." The post, published the same day, confirms that Research is available on desktop.
Outlier scores
At the centre of Research is a ranking of videos that do much better than their channels usually do. The post defines Outlier videos as "Videos that are performing significantly above a channel's typical averages to see what topics, hooks, and packaging resonate." The video gives a number: creators can "spot breakout outlier videos across your niche that are significantly outperforming a channel's normal baseline, like 5x outlier score and really resonating with audiences."
YouTube's help article "Research content & find trends" spells out the arithmetic. According to the page, an outlier is a video that gets significantly more traffic than the channel's average from previous videos, and a score of 5x on a long-form video means it drew five times the views of the channel's earlier long-form uploads. The comparison is format against format. The page does not give a time window. A screenshot in the Community post shows a results page headed "Getting more views than usual", with filter chips for Shorts and "Outlier score: >5x".
Outlier scores had surfaced in public before the launch. On August 5, 2026, Tubefilter reported that YouTube was testing a Research tab with a small number of users, citing a YouTube spokesperson, and that screenshots posted by Mario Joos, who works on retention for YouTube channels, showed multipliers ranging from 4x to 132x. Net Influencer reported in July that the score appeared to measure performance against the rest of a channel's output during a video's first seven days, while noting that Joos was unsure how YouTube calculates it. Neither the Community post nor the help article mentions a seven-day window.
Filters and the "Watched by my viewers" view
The video names three filters: format, "like videos or shorts," duration, and "watched by my viewers to see what your existing audience is already enjoying across YouTube." The post names two of them, "Watched by my viewers" and format, "Videos vs. Shorts." The help article lists eight in total: type, views, Watched by my viewers, outlier score, upload date, subscribers, duration and channel age. It describes the "Watched by my viewers" filter as showing what a channel's audience watched on other channels in the last month.
That last filter rests on data no outside tool can see: what a creator's own viewers watch elsewhere on YouTube. When Tubefilter reported the test in August, Joos singled it out as the point where YouTube beats any other tool.
Ask Studio reads the results
Research also feeds Ask Studio. In the video, the assistant can "summarize recurring title patterns and packaging strategies behind those top breakout videos." The post makes the same claim: "Ask Studio can uncover recurring title patterns and packaging strategies behind top-performing content." The help article adds that Ask Studio has access to the same YouTube-wide search that powers Research. In the screenshot, an "Analyze videos" button opens a side panel headed "Title patterns", which describes title patterns from a sample of outlier videos with 2.56 million total views, followed by sections titled "Top performers" and "Why this works."
The emphasis on packaging, meaning titles and thumbnails, follows what YouTube has told creators about distribution. In a Creator Insider interview in September, Todd Beaupré said that a channel's videos typically get a click-through rate of about 10% or less from its own subscribers. When a recommender system puts a video in front of a viewer, the title and thumbnail are most of what that viewer sees before deciding.
Research is the latest in a series of changes to how YouTube surfaces what is popular. The company closed its public Trending page on July 21, 2025, pointing viewers to category charts instead. In an April 2025 interview, a YouTube Studio product director described the Studio Inspiration tab as having been split off from trends.
Ask Studio on the phone
"Did you know Ask Studio is launching on mobile inside the YouTube Studio app for Android and iOS, bringing your conversational creative partner right to your phone?" the video opens. The post is more direct: "You can now access Ask Studio directly on your phone in the YouTube Studio mobile app on both Android and iPhone."
According to the video, the mobile version summarises how recent uploads are doing, including audience sentiment and top comments: "Analyze how recent uploads are performing with quick summaries of audience sentiment and top comments." Creators can "Capture ideas, outline, scripts, and draft titles on the fly without waiting to go back to your computer." Prompts can be spoken rather than typed, a feature the chapter list calls "Voice-to-text prompts & mobile sync." Creators can attach specific videos or Shorts from their channel to the conversation: "Attach specific videos or shorts from your channel to get targeted comment summaries, retention diagnostics, or follow-up ideas, and conversations automatically sync between mobile and desktop, so you can keep the conversation going no matter what device you're working on."
YouTube first presented Ask Studio at Made on YouTube in September 2025 as a conversational tool for analytics, community and ideas. Since then it has gained generative thumbnails on desktop, which were live globally by July 2026, and, from November 6, the ability to hand some creators over to a live human agent. The mobile version was first promised at Made on YouTube 2026, where the presenter said only that Ask Studio was coming to mobile, with no date, according to PPC Land's coverage at the time.
YouTube's help page on Ask Studio says the assistant is available to most YouTube creators globally, with three exclusions: Official Artist Channels, channels set as made for kids, and creators under 18. The page does not list supported languages.
Images enter the chat
The second Ask Studio change works on both platforms. "Additionally, you can now upload up to 10 images at once into Ask Studio," according to the post, which names two uses: "Brainstorm thumbnail concepts and compare variants side by side" and "Share reference graphics to inspire your next set design or graphic overlay."
The video opens this segment hypothetically too, with "Imagine you could add visual context to your chats on Ask Studio mobile and desktop by uploading thumbnail concepts, screenshots, or sketches to brainstorm and create even faster", before switching to instructions. "To get started, just hit the plus attachment button on the bottom left corner of your chat box." The limit is the same as in the post: "For thumbnail ideation, you can upload up to 10 images at once, including sketches, mood boards, or graphics to generate new concepts and compare thumbnail variants side by side." A second use is aimed at editors: "You can also upload still frames from your work in progress edit to get targeted notes on framing, composition before exporting."
One of the post's mobile screenshots shows a prompt reading "Create a thumbnail for this video using the style of this image" with two images attached, and Ask Studio replying that it has developed two distinct thumbnail options. Another shows the opening screen offering "Analyze channel performance", "Create a thumbnail" and "Brainstorm video ideas" as starting points.
What happens to the images
The video gives the privacy rule in a single sentence: "Uploaded images stay strictly private to your active session and are automatically deleted after 30 days." The post does not repeat it. The Ask Studio help page puts the 30 days in a wider frame: conversations are kept for up to 30 days, conversations connected to a channel are deleted automatically after 30 days, and human reviewers may read conversations. The video's phrase "strictly private" does not address that review. In the Research screenshot, the Ask Studio panel carries the line "AI can make mistakes. You are responsible for the content you publish."
Thumbnails are where YouTube has built most of its testing tools. Creators with advanced features have been able to test up to three titles, thumbnails or combinations on long-form videos since December 2025, with the winner chosen by watch time per impression. Ask Studio's image uploads sit earlier in that chain, before a thumbnail exists, while A/B testing on live audiences comes after.
The four changes at a glance
Trends tab and Research tab compared
How the features work, according to YouTube
- Ask Studio on mobile. According to the post, Ask Studio is reached inside the YouTube Studio mobile app on Android and iPhone. The video says prompts can be typed or spoken, specific videos or Shorts can be attached, and conversations sync between the phone and desktop.
- Uploading images. According to the video, the upload starts from the plus attachment button in the bottom left corner of the chat box. Up to 10 images can be added at once, on desktop and mobile.
- Image retention. According to the video, uploaded images stay private to the active session and are deleted automatically after 30 days. The help page says conversations are kept for up to 30 days and may be read by human reviewers.
- Opening Research. According to the help article, Research is reached on a computer by selecting Insights in the left menu of Studio and then Research in the top menu. A topic is entered in the search bar, and hovering over a result and selecting "More like this" saves its title as a search chip.
- Reading outlier scores. According to the help article, the score compares a video's views with the channel's earlier uploads in the same format, so 5x on a long-form video means five times the views of previous long-form uploads.
- Filtering. According to the help article, results can be narrowed by type, views, Watched by my viewers (what the audience watched on other channels in the last month), outlier score, upload date, subscribers, duration and channel age.
- Opening Insights. According to the help page, Insights is selected from the left menu of Studio on desktop for channel-level data, or through Content and then Insights for a single video. According to the video, selecting any card opens detailed tables and custom date ranges.
- Advanced analytics. According to the video, advanced analytics and real-time data are unchanged. The post says the existing Analytics tools remain fully available in Studio.
Why this matters for marketers
YouTube Studio is where creator channel data starts. Figures from it end up in media kits, sponsorship negotiations and campaign wrap reports. When the main screen moves from charts and tabs to shelves and sentences, the first figures a creator sees, and the screenshots a partner receives, can change even though the underlying data does not. The advanced view stays, according to YouTube. The convenience of the old tabbed layout, as the most-liked comment under the video shows, may not.
The written explanations are produced by YouTube's own systems. A card that says "Views are up thanks to loyal viewers" is a judgement about cause, not a raw count, and neither the post nor the video explains how those judgements are generated or checked. For an industry already dealing with a new definition of a view from August 24, under which a view counts from the moment playback begins, and the casual and regular viewer categories introduced in July 2025, plain-language summaries add another interpretive layer between the data and the people paying for it.
Research shifts competitive analysis inside the platform. Outside tools and open-source projects, including a Gemini-based YouTube Topic Insights project published in Google's marketing solutions GitHub organisation, have tried to identify which topics are breaking out. YouTube's version can filter by what a channel's own audience watched elsewhere in the past month, which only YouTube holds. For brands planning creator partnerships, the outlier score also offers a ready-made way to find videos that beat their channel's norm, though it measures views, not audience quality or sales.
The direction since September 2025 is consistent: more of the creative process runs through AI tools that YouTube builds into Studio, from AI comment search to generative thumbnails and now brainstorming on a phone. YouTube has also said it will let creators edit Shorts by chatting with Gemini in early 2027.
What the sources do not say
Neither the post nor the video defines "eligible creators" for Ask Studio, image uploads or the Insights card beyond the Help Center exclusions, or lists languages. Neither says whether Research or the Insights layout will reach the mobile app, or what happened to saved Trends keywords. The help article gives no time window for outlier scores, and none of the sources explains how the plain-language summaries are generated or how often they are wrong.
Key facts
- Products and features: Ask Studio on mobile (YouTube Studio app, Android and iPhone); image uploads in Ask Studio (up to 10 images at once); Research (replaces the Trends tab, desktop); Insights (replaces the Analytics page name on desktop, adds plain-language summaries).
- Availability, per TeamYouTube: "Ask Studio and Image Uploads are now available to eligible creators globally across desktop and the Studio mobile app, and Research and Insights are available on desktop devices."
- Unchanged, per the video: advanced analytics and real-time data.
- Image retention, per the video: private to the active session, deleted automatically after 30 days.
- Outlier score, per the Help Center: views compared with the channel's earlier uploads in the same format; 5x means five times the views.
- Ask Studio exclusions, per the Help Center: Official Artist Channels, made for kids channels, creators under 18.
- Video: "New! Ask Studio on Mobile, Image Uploads, Research Tab, Insights are the new Analytics", Creator Insider, published November 13, 2026, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3ZTA17BtpeQ. Ten chapters, about three minutes.
- Community post: "YouTube Studio Updates: Ask Studio on Mobile, Research and Revamped Insights!" by Dave (TeamYouTube), YouTube Help Community, November 13, 2026, https://support.google.com/youtube/thread/476500653.
- Help Center pages: "Research content & find trends" (answer 17232321); "Get started with YouTube Insights" (answer 9002587); "Learn about Ask Studio in YouTube Studio" (answer 16291691). None carries a date.

Summary
Who: YouTube, through TeamYouTube's Help Community post and the Creator Insider channel, and the creators who use YouTube Studio, along with the brands and agencies that rely on creator data.
What: Ask Studio now runs in the YouTube Studio mobile app on Android and iPhone and accepts up to 10 images at once. A Research tab replaces Trends and ranks outlier videos against their channel's own average. The Analytics page becomes Insights, with plain-language summaries, shelves of metrics and an Ask Studio card for eligible creators, while advanced analytics and real-time data stay unchanged.
When: Announced and made available on November 13, 2026, after a limited test reported in July 2026 and a demonstration at Made on YouTube on September 23, 2026.
Where: Globally for eligible creators in the case of Ask Studio and image uploads, on desktop and mobile. Research and Insights are on desktop only.
Why: According to YouTube, raw numbers and charts can be overwhelming, and the old Analytics system "just wasn't flexible enough to keep evolving and to focus on important metrics like audience segments." Research is meant to help creators validate ideas before filming, and Ask Studio on mobile lets them work away from a desk.
